newsitem.title: USA: No sign of wage-push inflation - Clinton economist.
newsitem.headline: No sign of wage-push inflation - Clinton economist.

text.p: White House chief economist Joseph Stiglitz said on Tuesday he saw no sign of wage-push inflation and suggested that the U.S. unemployment rate could fall a bit further without fanning price pressures.

In an interview with Reuters during the Democratic Party's national convention, Stiglitz also laid out President Clinton's economic agenda for a second term, stressing among other things the importance of balancing the budget and promoting exports.

"The first term's agenda was focused on getting the economy back to full employment, restoring it from a state that was really not very healthy," the chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers said. "Now we are much better poised to focus on long-term economic growth."

Unemployment in August was 5.4 percent, hovering just above a six-year low. Stiglitz reckoned that full employment might be in the range of a 5.2 to 5.7 percent jobless rate, indicating the economy might have further room to run without pushing up inflation.
"Some people would suggest you'd want to explore gradually how low you can go (on unemployment)," he said, adding, "There is no evidence that we stand on a precipice."

Federal Reserve officials said earlier this year that the central bank was doing just what Stiglitz had suggested, running a monetary experiment to see how low unemployment could fall. But lately, some Fed officials have begun to worry that they may have gone too far and have started to campaign for higher interest rates to head off what they see as incoming inflation.
Stiglitz said that wages have begun to rise, but added that the growth of overall worker compensation has remained moderate, thanks to contained health care costs.
"I really don't think at the present time I see inflationary pressures there," he added.

Looking further down the road, Stiglitz said Clinton intended to use a second term to build on the economic achievements of his first four years in office and push ahead into new areas aimed at promoting the economy's long-term growth prospects.
Clinton has a healthy lead over his Republican rival Bob Dole in the opinion polls with just over 2-1/2 months to go until the November 5 election.
Stiglitz said that Clinton's number one macro-economic priority if he wins re-election will be balancing the budget.

The president has promised to eliminate the deficit by the year 2002, but Stiglitz said Clinton may be able to accomplish that even earlier because the 1996 budget numbers have turned out better than expected.
"The way the numbers are coming in, it looks like it will be 2001 or sooner," he said.
The administration will also continue to promote U.S. exports "very strongly", pressing to open up foreign markets to American goods, according to Stiglitz.

Exports have surged during Clinton's tenure, but some economists have ascribed that to a steep depreciation of the dollar during the president's first two years in office, rather than to an improvement in underlying U.S. competitiveness.
Stiglitz brushed aside those arguments, saying the dollar has not moved that much in trade weighted terms, although it has fluctuated widely against the Japanese yen.
"They're over-exaggerating the role of exchange rates," he said.
Other measures planned by Clinton for a second term include promotion of competition, through such steps as banking reform, and measures to improve education and worker training.
